summary:
Starpulse is a health tracking app for astronauts on long missions. Most health apps focus on today’s numbers, but in space the bigger problem is slow change: sleep slipping, blood pressure creeping up, bone and muscle loss. Those are easy to miss day to day.

When astronauts open Starpulse, they start on a dashboard showing an overview of their health across five areas: behavioral, cardiovascular, body, vision and radiation. A spider graph scores each area and flags anything outside its healthy range. Tapping an area shows the metrics behind it, each compared to the astronaut’s own pre-flight baseline and Earth ranges, so trends show up early. A quick daily check-in takes about 30 seconds, and the dashboard also shows environmental data from NASA’s RR-28 dataset.

We added streaks and crew goals to keep people logging. Points come from logging, not from the results, so there’s no reason to skip a bad day. Crewmates only see who checked in, never anyone’s health data.
details:
When astronauts open Starpulse, they start on a dashboard showing an overview of their health across five areas: behavioral, cardiovascular, body, vision and radiation. Each area gets a score out of 100 on a spider graph, and anything outside its healthy range shows up in orange. The dashboard also shows today’s check-in progress, their logging streak, alerts, and environmental data (CO₂, temperature and humidity) from NASA’s RR-28 dataset.

Tapping an area opens a second spider graph with the metrics inside it. Tapping a metric opens its detail page, with a trend chart (7 days, 30 days or the whole mission) compared with the astronaut’s pre-flight baseline and the Earth range, plus a quick way to log a new reading. We track 12 metrics: sleep, mood, fatigue, stress, heart rate, blood pressure, HRV, blood oxygen, exercise, body mass, hydration and estimated bone density.

Each day there’s a six-question check-in. Anything already synced from a wearable is filled in, so most days it’s two or three taps. Every reading feeds back into the charts and scores right away.

Benefits

  • Slow changes become easy to see. Sleep slipping or blood pressure creeping up shows up as a trend instead of getting lost day to day.
  • Astronauts compare themselves to their own pre-flight baseline, not only a general Earth average, since what’s normal for one person isn’t for another.
  • Alerts say what to do next, like re-measuring blood pressure, instead of just flagging a number.
  • Logging takes about 30 seconds a day, so it’s realistic to keep up on a busy schedule.

Intended impact

The health changes that matter most in space happen slowly: bone loss, fluid shifts, sleep loss and vision changes. On longer missions, astronauts can’t count on a quick answer from the ground. We want Starpulse to help them catch those changes early and handle more of their own health monitoring. The longer-term goal is a habit of consistent, honest logging that gives a clearer picture of crew health over a whole mission.

Tools, languages and software

  • Figma for research boards, wireframes, the style guide and the clickable prototype
  • TypeScript, React and Vite for the app, with custom SVG charts
  • GitHub and GitHub Actions to deploy to star-pulse.earth
  • NASA’s RR-28 telemetry data, averaged by the hour for the environmental charts
  • Claude to help with research, design and code

The demo can run on a browser.

How Starpulse stands out

  • Points are for showing up, not for good numbers. Logging a bad blood pressure reading earns the same as a good one, because hiding bad data is the last thing you want on a mission.
  • The crew features are built around privacy. Crewmates see who checked in and their streaks, never anyone’s health data.
  • The two-level spider graph gives one picture of your overall health, and one tap shows what’s behind it.

Factors we considered

  • Research first: we read the NASA Human Research Program risk pages and the Canadian Space Agency resources from the challenge, then ranked which health areas an app could actually help with.
  • What makes people log: we looked at health apps people already use (Apple Health, Oura, Whoop, Samsung Health, Strava, Bearable and Daylio) to see what makes daily logging stick and what makes it feel like a chore.
  • Time: astronauts are busy, so the check-in is short and the app stays quiet unless something needs attention.
  • Accessibility: status is shown with color, an icon and a word together, so it still works for color-blind users.
  • Honest data: the health data in the demo is simulated, and the environmental section says the RR-28 data is historical research telemetry, not live station readings.
